But hours later, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating the company's terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, had taken responsibility for imposing the curbs. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," Musk said on X. Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said on the Telegram app that the country is "physically unable" to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations. Ukraine's general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment. Starshield's problems occurred after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped Starshield operations at speeds of 160 kph (100 mph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations. "The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Telegram before Musk's statement. According to Zelenskiy, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph. Ukraine does not rely on Starlink for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries. It operates at speeds no higher than 70-90 kph, Beskrestnov said. But it remains [USN:L6N4690ON TEXT:"vital"] for frontline communications, and the deployment of fast Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year. LIMITATIONS ORDER The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence. Both Musk and US officials said publicly that any decisions on Starlink and Starshield limitations could only have been taken by the other. Reuters has reported that the [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"order to throttle"] Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, US administrations had several times [USN:L4N4691IH TEXT:"asked SpaceX"] to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said. On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "[USN:L6N4690ZQ TEXT:"get it straightened out"]".

item.title: Houthis say they targeted Saudi oil sites; attacks reported in Aden
item.description: Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified. On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war , Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted. SAUDIS REPORT DEBRIS FROM INTERCEPTED MISSILES Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline. He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif. Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year. It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of the Rabigh oil refinery. Shortly after that, Houthis denied that they attacked Mecca and Medina, saying that their operations "target Saudi oil facilities and military bases." The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa. The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran . In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district. Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there. There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion. Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah. About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed. The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

item.title: Jordan king orders 'iron fist' response to deadly church attack
item.description: Jordan's King Abdullah ordered security forces on Saturday to respond with an "iron fist" as authorities searched for gunmen who opened fire and killed nine people during a church funeral service.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi
item.content:encoded: Jordan's King Abdullah ordered security forces on Saturday to respond with an "iron fist" as authorities searched for gunmen who opened fire and killed nine people during a church funeral service. The assailants [USN:L6N46A02E TEXT:"fired for several minutes"] in broad daylight at the church in Karak governorate on Friday, and also wounded 40 people in the rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority. Security was stepped up at malls, foreign embassies and other locations across the country, the US embassy in Amman said. 'A SENSE OF PANIC TOOK HOLD' A priest described how he and others ordered people to get to the ground at Saint George's Greek Orthodox church, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman. "A sense of panic took hold among those present," Theodoros Soueiss told Reuters. "The gunfire was indiscriminate, and you never knew where a bullet might land." King Abdullah condemned the "despicable terrorist act" as he chaired a National Security Council meeting and said there was no room for leniency when it comes to the lives of Jordanians, the royal court said. Such attacks are highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities there say they have foiled several Islamist plots in recent years. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack in the kingdom, a major partner with the US in the fight against militant groups. Officials have said it is too early to determine whether the attackers had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. "A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word," said Tarek Ammarin at a hospital where the wounded were being treated. A relative of Ammarin's was injured in the attack. Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. Jordan has been among the US allies in the Middle East to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February. Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a long list of officials condemning what they called an attack by extremist terrorists. "God willing, this country will remain secure," he said.

item.title: North Korea's Kim crosses new bridge into China as trade ties warm
item.description: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties.
item.dc:creator: Joyce Lee, Eduardo Baptista
item.content:encoded: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties. Kim was accompanied during his visit by China's fourth-highest-ranked official Wang Huning, who conveyed greetings from President Xi Jinping, the official Xinhua news agency said. Kim arrived in Dandong via the [USN:L6N46004I TEXT:"New Yalu River Bridge"] connecting North Korea and China , a South Korean government official said on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly. The new bridge is expected to help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development. Its official opening this month is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, after two summits between their leaders in the past 13 months. China, which fought alongside North Korea in the 1950-1953 Korean War, remains Pyongyang's main economic and diplomatic backer and accounts for most of its official trade. CHINESE TV SHOWS KIM WALKING ON BRIDGE But North Korea's deepening military ties with Russia since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine have led analysts to question whether Pyongyang is becoming less reliant on Beijing. Kim's trip nevertheless points to a renewed push by China and North Korea to bolster their economic relationship. South Korea's Yonhap news agency had earlier reported that Kim was expected to return to North Korea after Saturday's visit. Footage from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed Kim walking on the bridge, lined by people waving flags, towards North Korea. Xinhua said Wang accompanied Kim to a Korean War memorial in Dandong, where the North Korean leader paid tribute to Chinese People's Volunteer Army soldiers who fought alongside North Korea during the three-year conflict. Kim also toured a Dandong [USN:RTV844HDK TEXT:"automobile factory"], it said. NEW YALU RIVER BRIDGE BOOSTS BILATERAL TIES China and North Korea opened the 3 km (2 mile) New Yalu River Bridge, their most significant [USN:L1N46103M TEXT:"land border crossing"], this month after a long delay, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and pandemic-related disruptions. "Kim has given his imprimatur to bilateral trade by crossing the New Yalu River Bridge to enter China," said Christopher Green, a Korea specialist at Leiden University in the Netherlands, saying the delayed opening had shown how dysfunctional the relationship had become. During a meeting on Saturday, Wang told Kim that China was ready to use the bridge's opening to expand personnel exchanges and economic and trade cooperation, Xinhua said. A visit by Kim now is consistent with the current phase of closer economic ties and more frequent high-level exchanges between China and North Korea, said Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think-tank in Shenyang. "The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics," Lu said. "With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further." TRUMP WAITS FOR KIM TO ENGAGE Kim's last known visit to China was in September 2025, to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, when he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Xi made a [USN:L1N42G106 TEXT:"state visit"] to North Korea in June. US President Donald Trump has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but US and South Korean officials see [USN:L1N4690EW TEXT:"fading chances"] of him meeting Kim this year, Reuters reported on Friday. China hosts a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum next month in Shenzhen, which Trump is expected to attend.

item.title: How Trump's energy dominance turned into hubris
item.description: It was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer that enabled Trump to pursue foreign-policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, [USN:L1N3Q1127 TEXT:"“energy dominance”"] was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections . Ironically, it was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career. In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance. Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices. What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris. UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country's onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets. US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system. Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine. On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to [USN:S0N3NI004 TEXT:"“unleash American energy”"], prioritising oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables. Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”. ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy. The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region. In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war , and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the [USN:L6N45E05Y TEXT:"Arctic territory"]. The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after [USN:L6N3Y407K TEXT:"Washington removed Venezuelan President"] Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation. The US subsequently [USN:L1N3ZM1KL TEXT:"took control"] of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test. THE IRAN QUAGMIRE The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief. Those assumptions have not aged well. The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption. This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude peaking at $118 a barrel in March. That was well below the record [USN:L03220220 TEXT:"$145 reached in 2008"], when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock. Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110. The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington's Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unravelled longstanding supply routes and sent [USN:L6N45R160 TEXT:"shipping prices"] skyrocketing. Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind. PAIN AT THE PUMP In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market. Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year. But that protection has been far from ironclad. US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while [USN:L1N45211Q TEXT:"diesel"] surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed. Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3. The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including [USN:L6N44M0V8 TEXT:"easing biofuel blending mandates"] and, most controversially, reaching a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel supply agreement"] with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices. Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households. While Trump briefly floated the idea of a [USN:L6N45E0T3 TEXT:"diesel export ban"], officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics. ‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’ The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centres underpinning the artificial intelligence race. But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security. For countries dependent on imports, particularly [USN:L6N3ZY18D TEXT:"many in Asia"], the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity. That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years. Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had baulked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas. But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home. Hubris can be a dangerous thing. (The opinions expressed here are those of Ron Bousso , a columnist for Reuters.) Enjoying this column? item.title: Fire devastates former Nazi guest house 'Eagle's Nest'
item.description: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday. Around 200 firefighters and emergency workers near Berchtesgaden in Bavaria were battling the flames after the building, known as the Kehlsteinhaus, caught fire on Friday, police said. Built in 1938 as a guest house for Nazi officials and their guests, the building sits in a spectacular Alpine setting above Berchtesgaden. Adolf Hitler used it occasionally, earning it the nickname "Hitler's Tea House". It is separate from his nearby summer residence, the Berghof. Bild newspaper quoted a police spokesperson as saying the building, preserved after World War Two as a historical monument linked to the Nazi era, had been so badly damaged that it "could probably not be saved". Police said earlier they had detained a man near the site but had not yet established the cause of the fire. "Whether the person is linked to the fire is currently the subject of a criminal investigation," Bavarian police said in a statement.

item.title: US accuses government contractor of leaking classified info to girlfriend's Substack
item.description: The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Trotta
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter. The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, 42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information. A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment. “As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement. “That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably,” Eisenberg said. Brinksman held a top secret security clearance while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said. According to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence. The affidavit only identifies the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles she published. "A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads. That quote appears in a September 28 piece published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez. "Over the past year, I’ve published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets before she launched the newsletter. Chávez did not respond to an email message seeking comment. Investigators allege that on at least five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, some at the top secret level. On some of those dates, Chávez published articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA. According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having worked as a US State Department foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement. The State Department declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: US has for years asked Musk to alter Starlink service in Ukraine, Middle East, sources say
item.description: The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe.
item.dc:creator: Erin Banco, Joey Roulette
item.content:encoded: Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter. During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials. Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time. The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies. The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy. The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists. STARSHIELD RESTRICTIONS HOBBLE UKRAINE MILITARY Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country’s military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks. Reuters has reported that [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"the order to throttle Starshield"] came from inside the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order. The White House, contacted for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out." Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it." SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).” Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX. "Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said. For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products. Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine. MUSK'S INFLUENCE RAISES UNCERTAINTY Musk's role as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services. The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy. "He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said. In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting , Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials. Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war. The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said. Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability, they said. They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals. Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries. In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said. In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials. In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals. Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials. In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials. Starlink terminals were moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many were transferred. The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran. Iran's delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Fear factory
item.description: How filmmakers turn psychological triggers, practical effects and modest budgets into some of Hollywood's most profitable movies
item.dc:creator: Tiana McGee, Anurag Rao, Travis Hartman
item.content:encoded: Before the film, a cinema fills with rows of seats. Choose a rating, put on headphones, and watch a red door with a peephole loom closer. The camera pushes through the peephole into a dark hallway, where something is waiting. Reduce motion R **May contain jump scares PG Click headphones to turn sound on Before every horror film comes a warning. Not about what’s on the screen; about what it might do to you. Choose your experience wisely. Horror is something you experience, not just watch. You sit back, the lights dim, and you plunge into darkness. A feeling of unease starts to settle on you, but you can’t look away. Instead, Horror invites you to look closer. Something looks off. Everything is too quiet. Your body tenses. Your toes curl. You feel like the smallest thing in the room. Your heart is pounding in your chest and then – Just a glimpse and then it’s gone. But you know it’s still there. A creature. An unknown danger. A silent promise waiting to be kept. Fear Factory How filmmakers turn psychological triggers, practical effects and modest budgets into some of Hollywood's most profitable movies By Tiana McGee , Anurag Rao and Travis Hartman Published October 23, 2026 Fear Factory By Tiana McGee , Anurag Rao and Travis Hartman Published Oct. 23, 2026 06:00 AM EDT Horror movies have seen a dramatic rise in both critical acclaim and financial success. The genre has long been one of the safer box-office bets for studios wringing big returns out of modest budgets. Now, in an industry still recovering from the pandemic, that reliability has become a beacon. Because of this dependability, Michelle Martinez, a senior instructor at Arizona State University’s Film and Media Studies program, sees horror as Hollywood’s lifeline. “That’s how we persist,” she said. “Horror film has always been a ‘yes and’ sport. It’s always been low-budget. Nobody took it seriously until now, really.” We're gonna need a bigger box office Horror films are taking up a larger chunk of the domestic box office. In recent years, a single film has dominated each year’s share. This year’s summer blockbuster Obsession made up almost 29% of horror’s overall box office as of July. 5%10%15%20%0201220132014201520162017201820192020202120222023202420252026 Share of total box office The year's #1 horror film All other horror films A gash is cut across the top of the chart and blood falls out of it into fifteen pools, one per year from 2012 to 2026. Pool depth is horror’s share of total domestic box office, rising from 5.9% in 2012 to 18.2% in 2026, on an axis reading 50% at the cut down to zero at the floor. The bright blood at the foot of each pool is that year’s #1 horror film. Note: Data as of July; box office numbers are for the U.S. & Canada Source: Rentrak Horror isn’t just succeeding at the box office; critics are taking notice as well. Sinners , directed by Ryan Coogler, set in Jim Crow-era Mississippi Delta in 1932, received a record 16 Oscar nominations and earned Michael B. Jordan his first Oscar for Best Actor, marking a distinct return for the genre as a critic darling. In the 1970s and 80s, the slasher subgenre dominated the scene after the success of Halloween in 1978. The rise of VHS helped horror movies with limited releases find much-needed permanent homes on video store shelves, giving audiences greater access and opening the door for films to become cult classics. At the 64th Academy Awards in 1992, The Silence of the Lambs became the first and currently only horror film to win Best Picture. However, the 2000s marked a lull for the genre until 2017, when Jordan Peele’s Get Out seemed to announce a shift. All eyes on horror Horror films began to gain critical acclaim in the 1970s with The Exorcist . However, horror film award counts dropped off after 2000, until Get Out sparked a resurgence that continues today. Source: OMDb (Metacritic aggregate), matched against IMDb Horror-tagged titles. So, what does it mean to make art designed to scare people? Nine ways the camera works on you Different camera techniques have long been one of the most effective tools for unsettling audiences. Here are nine common examples: Dolly zoom Dutch angle Bird's eye view Mirrors Close-ups Off-center subjects Camera behind something POV Shaky cam The dolly zoom pulls you into the character’s mindset during tense moments Creative camera placement adds tension and suspense A bird’s eye view offers distance, so you watch the drama unfold A Dutch angle tilts the shot to signal unease POV shots immerse you in the character’s perspective All movies are built on balancing moments of tension with moments of release or relaxation for viewers. In horror movies, this becomes especially important. Moments of peace, even mundane ones, can lure the audience into a false sense of security. A lull can trick you into letting your guard down before the next high-tension moment/scare. With jump scares, there are often moments of silence or softness before the scare. After these moments, a sudden, sharp musical chord or loud sound effect known as the sting typically occurs at the same moment the threat/danger appears. “It might open with some gore just to set the tone or have a little early pre-scare just to prime you,” Martinez said. “So that you’re ready for the bigger build.” Prepare for a SCARE! Each mark below represents a jumpscare. Over the film’s two-hour runtime, it has 11 scares, but they don’t arrive on a schedule. Three jump scares in 4 minutesTwo scares 18 seconds apart015m30m45m60m75m90m105m120m A single horizontal strip spanning the 122-minute runtime of The Exorcist, with a vertical tick at each of its 11 cataloged jump scares. The first arrives 11 minutes in, three cluster in a four-minute burst around the 30-minute mark, the longest calm runs 25 minutes through the second hour, and the final two land 18 seconds apart with 10 minutes of film still to go. Note: whenjumpscare.com rates none of these 11 as major; that is a judgment about how each moment is staged, not a verdict on how frightening the film is. Scare timestamps and severity are its editorial judgment Source: whenjumpscare.com With these moments of tension and release, less is more. In many movies with higher Metacritic ratings or critical acclaim, there are fewer jump scares per hour. The Scaring Horror films, plotted by how often they make you jump. Films with more scares per hour tend to score worse on average. Scores drift down as scare density rises, but the cloud is wide at every density. Oscar winners such as Alien, Jaws and Get Out sit high on the score axis at a range of densities. Note: One dot per film; 695 films with at least one cataloged jumpscare, so scare-free horror is absent. Rate is scares divided by runtime. Correlation only — dense jumpscares are also the house style of low-budget and late-franchise horror, which critics mark down for many reasons at once. Oscar nominees and winners cover all categories, not just the top awards. Source: whenjumpscare.com for scare timestamps, Metacritic for scores, Academy Awards database for nominations Sound amplifies the menace of the movie, seen or unseen. The score, and other sounds that occur outside the world of the story, can be used to manipulate you into feeling tense in moments where you may not even notice it consciously. Sounds that do exist in the world of the film, whispers or floorboards creaking, suggest that something is not as it should be. Lighting, too, is a pivotal choice for making horror work. Shadows and darkness keep things from the audience, letting them imagine the worst. Horror often uses what’s just out of reach to scare and disturb you. Click to turn out the lights The genre works well as a powerful lens for telling larger stories. Horror, like many other art forms, can reflect societal issues, offering a cathartic way to process hardship and trauma across different communities. By transforming real experiences into frightening yet safe scenarios, horror lets us confront hard topics in a controlled environment. Carrie , a movie based on Stephen King’s novel about a bullied high school girl raised by a fanatically religious and abusive mother, is a front-of-mind example for Martinez. The 1974 novel and the Brian De Palma film are often connected to the landmark abortion rights ruling of Roe v. Wade a year earlier, as both express themes of bodily autonomy and the consequences of “the repressing of female power.” Get Out serves as a social commentary on race and Black exploitation. Released in 2017, the film reflects the evolving discussions around race relations and systemic racism at the time. And films like the summer blockbuster Obsession return to questions of autonomy and critique modern dating culture, turning the “Nice Guy” trope on its head. Horror can also give the audience a safe space to work through emotion. Martinez finds that in her classes, it comes up a lot. “If you’re somebody that’s grieving and you go watch a horror film, it helps you push out that wave of grief,” She said. “When you have art that makes you feel […] It helps you reset. And I think for a lot of people, that’s why they really like it. With horror movies making a comeback in a big way, it’s easy to get swept up in the numbers and why they work, but for Martinez, it’s a bit simpler than that. Horror, she says, is a way to break out of the monotony of daily drudgery. “That’s what musicals do. That’s what horror does. It pinches you awake.” Edited by Julia Wolfe, Nick Zieminski

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Environ 1.200 Palestiniens déplacés à Hébron par une opération militaire israélienne JÉRUSALEM, 24 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée israélienne a contraint environ 1.200 Palestiniens à quitter leurs foyers à Hébron, en Cisjordanie occupée, a déclaré samedi un responsable palestinien, au lendemain d'une attaque qui a coûté la vie à deux soldats israéliens. Allemagne-Le "nid d'aigle" des nazis en Bavière incendié Le "nid d'aigle", ancienne résidence des dignitaires du régime nazi dans les montagnes bavaroises du sud de l'Allemagne, a pris feu vendredi soir et un suspect a été arrêté, a annoncé la police allemande. Le dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong Un en visite en Chine Le dirigeant de la Corée du Nord Kim Jong Un s'est rendu samedi en Chine en empruntant un pont tout juste ouvert entre les deux pays, a-t-on appris d'un responsable gouvernemental sud-coréen. L'Ukraine dit que Starlink refonctionne normalement Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense. La Russie et l'Ukraine acceptent un cessez-le-feu à Oleshky La Russie et l'Ukraine ont accepté de respecter un cessez-le-feu dans la ville ukrainienne d'Oleshky, occupée par la Russie, afin de permettre l'évacuation des civils pris au piège des combats, a annoncé vendredi la Maison blanche. L'Autriche expulse quatre diplomates russes, Moscou promet de répliquer Le ministère autrichien des Affaires étrangères a annoncé vendredi l'expulsion de quatre diplomates russes basés à Vienne en raison "d'activités incompatibles avec leur statut diplomatique", expression généralement employée pour des faits d'espionnage. La Corée du Sud propose à nouveau de discuter avec la Corée du Nord de la frontière terrestre Le ministère sud-coréen de la Défense a de nouveau proposé vendredi la tenue de pourparlers militaires avec la Corée du Nord, afin de s'accorder sur le tracé exact de la frontière terrestre entre les deux Corées et de réduire le risque d'affrontements accidentels. Le séisme au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés Le séisme de magnitude 7 survenu au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés, a annoncé vendredi le gouvernement local sur les réseaux sociaux. Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde menacées par les feux de forêt Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde, situées sur l'île indonésienne de Sulawesi, sont menacées par la chaleur et la fumée générées par les pires feux de forêt que le pays ait connus depuis plus d'une décennie, ont déclaré des chercheurs. Arabie saoudite: Nouveau report de forums internationaux à 2027 Deux nouveaux forums internationaux prévus en cette fin d'année en Arabie saoudite ont été reportés à 2027 en raison des attaques que lancent les Houthis, rebelles yéménites proches de l'Iran, sur le royaume, a déclaré vendredi l'Autorité générale des statistiques du pays.

item.content:encoded: La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque de Trappes prolongée PARIS, 24 octobre (Reuters) - La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque commise vendredi dans les Yvelines, qui a fait un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fillette de 12 ans, a été prolongée, a annoncé samedi le parquet national antiterroriste (PNAT). Jordan Bardella reconduit à la présidence du Rassemblement national ORLÉANS, Loiret, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Jordan Bardella a été reconduit samedi à la présidence du Rassemblement national, premier parti d'opposition de France, lors d'un congrès à Orléans (Loiret) où des personnalités de gauche ont participé de leur côté à une manifestation hostile à l'extrême droite. Veillée d'armes avant une nouvelle journée de manifestations, le dispositif sécuritaire renforcé La France se préparait vendredi à une nouvelle journée de manifestations à hauts risques samedi, une semaine après les violences et les pillages survenus en marge de défilés pour les conditions d'enseignement détériorées et contre la vie chère, obligeant l'exécutif à un sursaut. Le Pnat saisi après des tirs dans les Yvelines, sur place Macron dénonce un acte terroriste raciste Le président Emmanuel Macron s'est rendu à Trappes, dans les Yvelines, l'une des communes où un homme à bord d'un véhicule a tiré vendredi à l'arme automatique sur la voie publique, faisant un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fille de 12 ans. La tempête Austen balaie l'ouest de la France, 161.000 foyers privés d'électricité Quelque 161.000 foyers étaient privés d'électricité vendredi matin dans l'ouest de la France balayé par la tempête Austen, la première de l'automne, qui s'accompagne de vents violents, rapporte Enedis. Macron annonce l'interdiction des manifestations "sans légitimité" Les autorités interdiront dans les prochains jours les manifestations et regroupements sans "légitimité" et proposeront des "tracés alternatifs" aux syndicats pour protéger les centre-villes, a annoncé jeudi Emmanuel Macron, à deux jours d'un nouvel appel à manifester émanant notamment des "gilets jaunes". France: Premier décès lié au virus Shamonda, aucun risque sanitaire à ce jour selon les autorités Un patient est décédé début octobre du virus de Shamonda, une première en France et dans le monde, a annoncé jeudi le gouvernement, ajoutant qu'il n'y avait à ce stade aucun risque sanitaire pour la population générale au vu des connaissances sur ce virus. Cisjordanie: Les oliveraies de Palestiniens pillées lors d'attaques violentes de colons israéliens Ému aux larmes en se remémorant l'attaque contre son oliveraie par des colons israéliens il y a environ deux semaines près du village palestinien de Lubban al-Gharbi, en Cisjordanie, Ahmed Salem a déclaré s'être retrouvé impuissant, craignant d'être agressé s'il tentait d'intervenir pour protéger son exploitation. Gaza: Trois Palestiniens tués par des frappes israéliennes selon les secours Des frappes et des tirs israéliens ont tué au moins trois Palestiniens jeudi, dans deux incidents séparés survenus dans la bande Gaza, selon les autorités sanitaires locales. Serbie: La face autoritaire de Vucic en lumière avant les élections législatives Le militant serbe Marko Marjanovic rentrait du supermarché à Belgrade lorsque des officiers masqués l'ont embarqué dans un véhicule avant de l'amener dans le sous-sol d'un commissariat de police où il a été maintenu à l'isolement pendant deux jours sous un éclairage intense.
